A Christian at Damascus ([Acts 9:10](#Acts.9.10)). He became Paul’s instructor; but when or by what means he himself became a Christian we have no information. He was “a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt” at Damascus (22:12).

One of the members of the church at Jerusalem, who conspired with his wife Sapphira to deceive the brethren, and who fell down and immediately expired after he had uttered the falsehood ([Acts 5:5](#Acts.5.5)). By common agreement the members of the early Christian community devoted their property to the work of furthering the gospel and of assisting the poor and needy. …

The high priest before whom Paul was brought in the procuratorship of Felix ([Acts 23:2](#Acts.23.2), [5](#Acts.23.5), [24](#Acts.23.24)). He was so enraged at Paul’s noble declaration, “I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day,” that he commanded one of his attendants to smite him on the mouth. …
An answer; i.e., to “prayer”, the father of Shamgar, who was one of the judges of Israel ([Judg. 3:31](#Judg.3.31)).

Manliness, a Greek name; one of the apostles of our Lord. He was of Bethsaida in Galilee ([John 1:44](#John.1.44)), and was the brother of Simon Peter ([Matt. 4:18](#Matt.4.18); [10:2](#Matt.10.2)). On one occasion John the Baptist, whose disciple he then was, pointing to Jesus, said, “Behold the Lamb of God” ([John 1:40](#John.1.40)); and Andrew, hearing him, immediately became a follower of Jesus, the first of his disciples. After he had been led to recognize Jesus as the Messiah, his first care was to bring also his brother Simon to Jesus. …
Man-conquering, a Jewish Christian, the kinsman and fellowprisoner of Paul ([Rom. 16:7](#Rom.16.7)); “of note among the apostles.”
A Canaanitish chief who joined his forces with those of Abraham in pursuit of Chedorlaomer ([Gen. 14:13](#Gen.14.13), [24](#Gen.14.24)).

Grace, an aged widow, the daughter of Phanuel. She was a “prophetess,” like Miriam, Deborah, and Huldah ([2 Chr. 34:22](#2Chr.34.22)). After seven years of married life her husband died, and during her long widowhood she daily attended the temple services. When she was eighty-four years old, she entered the temple at the moment when the aged Simeon uttered his memorable words of praise and thanks to God that he had fulfilled his ancient promise in sending his Son into the world ([Luke 2:36](#Luke.2.36), [37](#Luke.2.37)).

Was high priest A.D. 7-14. In A.D. 25 Caiaphas, who had married the daughter of Annas ([John 18:13](#John.18.13)), was raised to that office, and probably Annas was now made president of the Sanhedrim, or deputy or coadjutor of the high priest, and thus was also called high priest along with Caiaphas ([Luke 3:2](#Luke.3.2)). By the Mosaic law the high-priesthood was held for life ([Num. 3:10](#Num.3.10)); and although Annas had been deposed by the Roman procurator, the Jews may still have regarded him as legally the high priest. …
A “faithful martyr” ([Rev. 2:13](#Rev.2.13)), of whom nothing more is certainly known.
A Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes ([Rom. 16:10](#Rom.16.10)), and styles “approved in Christ.”

A Jew “born at Alexandria,” a man well versed in the Scriptures and eloquent ([Acts 18:24](#Acts.18.24); R.V., “learned”). He came to Ephesus (about A.D. 49), where he spake “boldly” in the synagogue (18:26), although he did not know as yet that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah. Aquila and Priscilla instructed him more perfectly in “the way of God”, i.e., in the knowledge of Christ. He then proceeded to Corinth, where he met Paul ([Acts 18:27](#Acts.18.27); [19:1](#Acts.19.1)). He was there very useful in watering the good seed Paul had sown ([1 Cor. 1:12](#1Cor.1.12)), and in gaining many to Christ. …

Destruction, the Hebrew name (equivalent to the Greek Apollyon, i.e., destroyer) of “the angel of the bottomless pit” ([Rev. 9:11](#Rev.9.11)). It is rendered “destruction” in [Job 28:22](#Job.28.22); [31:12](#Job.31.12); [26:6](#Job.26.6); [Prov. 15:11](#Prov.15.11); [27:20](#Prov.27.20). In the last three of these passages the Revised Version retains the word “Abaddon.” We may regard this word as a personification of the idea of destruction, or as sheol, the realm of the dead.
Increasing, a female Christian at Colosse ([Philemon 1](#Phlm.1.1):2), supposed by some to have been the wife of Philemon.

Eagle, a native of Pontus, by occupation a tent-maker, whom Paul met on his first visit to Corinth ([Acts 18:2](#Acts.18.2)). Along with his wife Priscilla he had fled from Rome in consequence of a decree (A.D. 50) by Claudius commanding all Jews to leave the city. Paul sojourned with him at Corinth, and they wrought together at their common trade, making Cilician hair-cloth for tents. …
One of the sons of Beriah ([1 Chr. 8:15](#1Chr.8.15)).

The son of Shem ([Gen. 10:22](#Gen.10.22)); according to [Gen. 22:21](#Gen.22.21), a grandson of Nahor. In [Matt. 1:3](#Matt.1.3), [4](#Matt.1.4), and [Luke 3:33](#Luke.3.33), this word is the Greek form of Ram, the father of Amminadab ([1 Chr. 2:10](#1Chr.2.10)).

The son of Shem ([Gen. 10:22](#Gen.10.22)); according to [Gen. 22:21](#Gen.22.21), a grandson of Nahor. In [Matt. 1:3](#Matt.1.3), [4](#Matt.1.4), and [Luke 3:33](#Luke.3.33), this word is the Greek form of Ram, the father of Amminadab ([1 Chr. 2:10](#1Chr.2.10)).
Wild goat, a descendant of Seir the Horite ([Gen. 36:28](#Gen.36.28)).

Ruler of the people, son of Herod the Great, by Malthace, a Samaritan woman. He was educated along with his brother Antipas at Rome. He inherited from his father a third part of his kingdom viz., Idumea, Judea, and Samaria, and hence is called “king” ([Matt. 2:22](#Matt.2.22)). It was for fear of him that Joseph and Mary turned aside on their way back from Egypt. Till a few days before his death Herod had named Antipas as his successor, but in his last moments he named Archelaus.
Master of the horse, a “fellow-soldier” of Paul’s ([Philemon 1](#Phlm.1.1):2), whom he exhorts to renewed activity ([Col. 4:17](#Col.4.17)). He was a member of Philemon’s family, probably his son.
Descent, a grandson of Benjamin ([Num. 26:38-40](#Num.26.38)). In [1 Chr. 8:3](#1Chr.8.3) he is called Addar. His descendants are mentioned in [Num. 26:40](#Num.26.40).
Descendant, the last of the three sons of Caleb by his first wife Azubah ([1 Chr. 2:18](#1Chr.2.18)).

The father-in-law of Herod Antipas, and king of Arabia Petraea. His daughter returned to him on the occasion of her husband’s entering into an adulterous alliance with Herodias, the wife of Herod-Philip, his half-brother ([Luke 3:19](#Luke.3.19), [20](#Luke.3.20); [Mark 6:17](#Mark.6.17); [Matt. 14:3](#Matt.14.3)). This led to a war between Aretas and Herod Antipas. Herod’s army was wholly destroyed (A.D. 36). Aretas, taking advantage of the complications of the times on account of the death of the Emperor Tiberius (A.D. 37), took possession of Damascus ([2 Cor. 11:32](#2Cor.11.32); comp. [Acts 9:25](#Acts.9.25)). At this time Paul returned to Damascus from Arabia.
The lion, the name of one of the body-guard slain with Pekahiah at Samaria ([2 Kings 15:25](#2Kgs.15.25)) by the conspirator Pekah.
One of the chief men sent by Ezra to procure Levites for the sanctuary ([Ezra 8:16](#Ezra.8.16)).

A king of Ellasar who was confederate with Chedorlamer ([Gen. 14:1](#Gen.14.1), [9](#Gen.14.9)). The tablets recently discovered by Mr. Pinches (see CHALDEA) show the true reading is Eri-Aku of Larsa. This Elamite name meant “servant of the moon-god.” It was afterwards changed into Rimsin, “Have mercy, O moon-god.”

Best ruler, native of Thessalonica ([Acts 20:4](#Acts.20.4)), a companion of Paul ([Acts 19:29](#Acts.19.29); [27:2](#Acts.27.2)). He was Paul’s “fellow-prisoner” at Rome ([Col. 4:10](#Col.4.10); [Philemon 1](#Phlm.1.1):24).

([Gen. 10:17](#Gen.10.17); [1 Chr. 1:15](#1Chr.1.15)), a designation of certain descendants from the Phoenicians or Sidonians, the inhabitants of Arka, 12 miles north of Tripoli, opposite the northern extremity of Lebanon.
Inhabitant of a fortress, the first-named of the two sons of Saul and Rizpah. He was delivered up to the Gibeonites by David, and hanged by them ([2 Sam. 21:8](#2Sam.21.8), [9](#2Sam.21.9)).

Son of Shem, born the year after the Deluge. He died at the age of 438 years ([Gen. 11:10-13](#Gen.11.10); [1 Chr. 1:17](#1Chr.1.17), [18](#1Chr.1.18); [Luke 3:36](#Luke.3.36)). He dwelt in Mesopotamia, and became, according to the Jewish historian Josephus, the progenitor of the Chaldeans. The tendency is to recognize in the word the name of the country nearest the ancient domain of the Chaldeans. Some regard the word as an Egypticized form of the territorial name of Ur Kasdim, or Ur of the Chaldees.

The king mentioned in [Ezra 7:1](#Ezra.7.1), in the seventh year (B.C. 458) of whose reign Ezra led a second colony of Jews back to Jerusalem, was probably Longimanus, who reigned for forty years (B.C. 464-425); the grandson of Darius, who, fourteen years later, permitted Nehemiah to return and rebuild Jerusalem.
The king who obstructed the rebuilding of the temple ([Ezra 4:7](#Ezra.4.7)). He was probably the Smerdis of profane history.

Physician, son of Abijah and grandson of Rehoboam, was the third king of Judah. He was zealous in maintaining the true worship of God, and in rooting all idolatry, with its accompanying immoralities, out of the land ([1 Kings 15:8-14](#1Kgs.15.8)). The Lord gave him and his land rest and prosperity. It is recorded of him, however, that in his old age, when afflicted, he “sought not to the Lord, but to the physicians” (comp. [Jer. 17:5](#Jer.17.5)). He died in the forty-first year of his reign, greatly honoured by his people ([2 Chr. 16:1-13](#2Chr.16.1)), and was succeeded by his son Jehoshaphat.

Made by God, the youngest son of Zeruiah, David’s sister. He was celebrated for his swiftness of foot. When fighting against Ish-bosheth at Gibeon, in the army of his brother Joab, he was put to death by Abner, whom he pursued from the field of battle ([2 Sam. 2:18](#2Sam.2.18), [19](#2Sam.2.19)). He is mentioned among David’s thirty mighty men ([2 Sam. 23:24](#2Sam.23.24); [1 Chr. 11:26](#1Chr.11.26)). Others of the same name are mentioned ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8); [31:13](#2Chr.31.13); [Ezra 10:15](#Ezra.10.15)).

The son of Amoz ([Isa. 1:1](#Isa.1.1); [2:1](#Isa.2.1)), who was apparently a man of humble rank. His wife was called “the prophetess” (8:3), either because she was endowed with the prophetic gift, like Deborah ([Judg. 4:4](#Judg.4.4)) and Huldah ([2 Kings 22:14-20](#2Kgs.22.14)), or simply because she was the wife of “the prophet” ([Isa. 38:1](#Isa.38.1)). He had two sons, who bore symbolical names.

A Levite; one of the leaders of David’s choir ([1 Chr. 6:39](#1Chr.6.39)). [Psalms 50](#Ps.50) and 73-83 inclusive are attributed to him. He is mentioned along with David as skilled in music, and a “seer” ([2 Chr. 29:30](#2Chr.29.30)). The “sons of Asaph,” mentioned in [1 Chr. 25:1](#1Chr.25.1), [2](#1Chr.25.2) Chr. 20:14, and [Ezra 2:41](#Ezra.2.41), were his descendants, or more probably a class of poets or singers who recognized him as their master.
The “recorder” in the time of Hezekiah ([2 Kings 18:18](#2Kgs.18.18), [37](#2Kgs.18.37)).
The “keeper of the king’s forest,” to whom Nehemiah requested from Artaxerxes a “letter” that he might give him timber for the temple at Jerusalem ([Neh. 2:8](#Neh.2.8)).

An Egyptian name, meaning “gift of the sun-god”, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On or Heliopolis, wife of Joseph ([Gen. 41:45](#Gen.41.45)). She was the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim (50-52; 46:20).

Happy, Jacob’s eigth son; his mother was Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid ([Gen. 30:13](#Gen.30.13)). Of the tribe founded by him nothing is recorded beyond its holding a place in the list of the tribes (35:26; 46:17; [Ex. 1:4](#Exod.1.4), etc.) It increased in numbers twenty-nine percent, during the thirty-eight years’ wanderings. …

One of the three sons of Gomer ([Gen. 10:3](#Gen.10.3)), and founder of one of the tribes of the Japhetic race. They are mentioned in connection with Minni and Ararat, and hence their original seat must have been in Armenia ([Jer. 51:27](#Jer.51.27)), probably near the Black Sea, which, from their founder, was first called Axenus, and afterwards the Euxine.
The master of the eunuchs of Nebuchadnezzar ([Dan. 1:3](#Dan.1.3)), the “Rabsaris” of the court. His position was similar to that of the Kislar-aga of the modern Turkish sultans.

The moon goddess of the Phoenicians, representing the passive principle in nature, their principal female deity; frequently associated with the name of Baal, the sun-god, their chief male deity ([Judg. 10:6](#Judg.10.6); [1 Sam. 7:4](#1Sam.7.4); [12:10](#1Sam.12.10)). These names often occur in the plural (Ashtaroth, Baalim), probably as indicating either different statues or different modifications of the deities. This deity is spoken of as Ashtoreth of the Zidonians. …

Probably the same as Assur-bani-pal (Sardanapalos of the Greeks), styled the “great and noble” ([Ezra 4:10](#Ezra.4.10)), was the son and successor (B.C. 668) of Esar-haddon (q.v.). He was “luxurious, ambitious, and cruel, but a magnificent patron of literature.” He formed at Nineveh a library of clay tablets, numbering about 10,000. These are now mostly in the British Museum. They throw much light on the history and antiquities of Assyria.

Second son of Shem ([Gen. 10:22](#Gen.10.22); [1 Chr. 1:17](#1Chr.1.17)). He went from the land of Shinar and built Nineveh, etc. ([Gen. 10:11](#Gen.10.11), [12](#Gen.10.12)). He probably gave his name to Assyria, which is the usual translation of the word, although the form Asshur is sometimes retained ([Num. 24:22](#Num.24.22), [24](#Num.24.24); [Ezek. 27:23](#Ezek.27.23), etc.). In [Gen. 2:14](#Gen.2.14) “Assyria” ought to be “Asshur,” which was the original capital of Assyria, a city represented by the mounds of Kalah Sherghat, on the west bank of the Tigris. This city was founded by Bel-kap-kapu about B.C. 1700. At a later date the capital was shifted to Ninua, or Nineveh, now Koyunjik, on the eastern bank of the river.

The daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, and the wife of Jehoram, king of Judah ([2 Kings 8:18](#2Kgs.8.18)), who “walked in the ways of the house of Ahab” ([2 Chr. 21:6](#2Chr.21.6)), called “daughter” of Omri ([2 Kings 8:26](#2Kgs.8.26)). On the death of her husband and of her son Ahaziah, she resolved to seat herself on the vacant throne. She slew all Ahaziah’s children except Joash, the youngest ([2 Kings 11:1](#2Kgs.11.1), [2](#2Kgs.11.2)). After a reign of six years she was put to death in an insurrection ([2 Kings 11:20](#2Kgs.11.20); [2 Chr. 21:6](#2Chr.21.6); [22:10-12](#2Chr.22.10); [23:15](#2Chr.23.15)), stirred up among the people in connection with Josiah’s being crowned as king.

The cognomen of the first Roman emperor, C. Julius Caesar Octavianus, during whose reign Christ was born ([Luke 2:1](#Luke.2.1)). His decree that “all the world should be taxed” was the divinely ordered occasion of Jesus’ being born, according to prophecy ([Micah 5:2](#Mic.5.2)), in Bethlehem. This name being simply a title meaning “majesty” or “venerable,” first given to him by the senate (B.C. 27), was borne by succeeding emperors. Before his death (A.D. 14) he associated Tiberius with him in the empire ([Luke 3:1](#Luke.3.1)), by whom he was succeeded.

The original name of Abed-nego ([Dan. 1:6](#Dan.1.6), [7](#Dan.1.7), [11](#Dan.1.11), [16](#Dan.1.16)). He was of the royal family of Judah, and with his other two companions remarkable for his personal beauty and his intelligence as well as piety.
High priest in the reign of Uzziah, king of Judah ([2 Kings 14:21](#2Kgs.14.21); [2 Chr. 26:17-20](#2Chr.26.17)). He was contemporary with the prophets Isaiah, Amos, and Joel.
Son of Ethan, of the tribe of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:8](#1Chr.2.8)).
The son of Oded, a remarkable prophet in the days of Asa ([2 Chr. 15:1](#2Chr.15.1)). He stirred up the king and the people to a great national reformation.
One of the Levitical harpers in the temple ([1 Chr. 15:21](#1Chr.15.21)).
The father of Hoshea, who was made ruler over the Ephraimites ([1 Chr. 27:20](#1Chr.27.20)).
One who had charge of the temple offerings ([2 Chr. 31:13](#2Chr.31.13)).
Noble, a descendant of king Saul ([1 Chr. 8:37](#1Chr.8.37); [9:43](#1Chr.9.43), [44](#1Chr.9.44)).
One of David’s thirty warriors ([2 Sam. 23:31](#2Sam.23.31)).
An overseer over the royal treasury in the time of David and Solomon ([1 Chr. 27:25](#1Chr.27.25)).
The daughter of Shilhi, and mother of king Jehoshaphat ([1 Kings 22:42](#1Kgs.22.42)).
The father of Hananiah, a false prophet ([Jer. 28:1](#Jer.28.1)).
One of those who sealed the covenant with Jehovah on the return from Babylon ([Neh. 10:17](#Neh.10.17)).
The name appropriated to the principal male god of the Phoenicians. …
A Benjamite, son of Jehiel, the progenitor of the Gibeonites ([1 Chr. 8:30](#1Chr.8.30); [9:36](#1Chr.9.36)).
An overseer of “the olive trees and sycomore trees in the low plains” (the Shephelah) under David ([1 Chr. 27:28](#1Chr.27.28)).

Fly-lord, the god of the Philistines at Ekron ([2 Kings 1:2](#2Kgs.1.2), [3](#2Kgs.1.3), [16](#2Kgs.1.16)). This name was given to the god because he was supposed to be able to avert the plague of flies which in that region was to be feared. He was consulted by Ahaziah as to his recovery.
King of the Ammonites at the time of the Babylonian captivity ([Jer. 40:14](#Jer.40.14)). He hired Ishmael to slay Gedaliah who had been appointed governor over the cities of Judah.

One of the two sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, a captain in Saul’s army. He and his brother Rechab assassinated Ishbosheth ([2 Sam. 4:2](#2Sam.4.2)), and were on this account slain by David, and their mutilated bodies suspended over the pool at Hebron (5, 6, 12).
The father of Heled, who was one of David’s thirty heroes ([2 Sam. 23:29](#2Sam.23.29); [1 Chr. 11:30](#1Chr.11.30)).
Son of Hushai, another of Solomon’s purveyors ([1 Kings 4:16](#1Kgs.4.16)).

Bravery, the third king of the separate kingdom of Israel, and founder of its second dynasty ([1 Kings 15](#1Kgs.15); [16](#1Kgs.16); [2 Chr. 16:1-6](#2Chr.16.1)). He was the son of Ahijah of the tribe of Issachar. The city of Tirzah he made the capital of his kingdom, and there he was buried, after an eventful reign of twenty-four years ([1 Kings 15:33](#1Kgs.15.33)). On account of his idolatries his family was exterminated, according to the word of the prophet Jehu ([1 Kings 16:3](#1Kgs.16.3), [4](#1Kgs.16.4), [10-13](#1Kgs.16.10)).

Lord of the people; foreigner or glutton, as interpreted by others, the son of Beor, was a man of some rank among the Midianites ([Num. 31:8](#Num.31.8); comp. 16). He resided at Pethor ([Deut. 23:4](#Deut.23.4)), in Mesopotamia ([Num. 23:7](#Num.23.7)). It is evident that though dwelling among idolaters he had some knowledge of the true God; and was held in such reputation that it was supposed that he whom he blessed was blessed, and he whom he cursed was cursed. …
He has given a son, the father of the Babylonian king ([2 Kings 20:12](#2Kgs.20.12); [Isa. 39:1](#Isa.39.1)) Merodach-baladan (q.v.).

Empty; spoiler, a son of Zippor, and king of the Moabites ([Num. 22:2](#Num.22.2), [4](#Num.22.4)). From fear of the Israelites, who were encamped near the confines of his territory, he applied to Balaam (q.v.) to curse them; but in vain ([Josh. 24:9](#Josh.24.9)).
One of David’s thirty-seven warriors, a Gadite ([2 Sam. 23:36](#2Sam.23.36)).

I.e., son of Abba or of a father, a notorious robber whom Pilate proposed to condemn to death instead of Jesus, whom he wished to release, in accordance with the Roman custom ([John 18:40](#John.18.40); [Mark 15:7](#Mark.15.7); [Luke 23:19](#Luke.23.19)). But the Jews were so bent on the death of Jesus that they demanded that Barabbas should be pardoned ([Matt. 27:16-26](#Matt.27.16); [Acts 3:14](#Acts.3.14)). This Pilate did.
Whom God has blessed, a Buzite, the father of Elihu, one of Job’s friends ([Job 32:2](#Job.32.2), [6](#Job.32.6)).

Lightning, the son of Abinoam ([Judg. 4:6](#Judg.4.6)). At the summons of Deborah he made war against Jabin. She accompanied him into the battle, and gave the signal for the little army to make the attack; in which the host of Jabin was completely routed. The battle was fought ([Judg. 4:16](#Judg.4.16)) in the plain of Jezreel (q.v.). This deliverance of Israel is commemorated in [Judg. 5](#Judg.5). Barak’s faith is commended ([Heb. 11:32](#Heb.11.32)). “The character of Barak, though pious, does not seem to have been heroic. Like Gideon, and in a sense Samson, he is an illustration of the words in [Heb. 11:34](#Heb.11.34), ’Out of weakness were made strong.’”
Fugitive, one of Shemaiah’s five sons. Their father is counted along with them in [1 Chr. 3:22](#1Chr.3.22).
Painter, ([Ezra 2:53](#Ezra.2.53); [Neh. 7:55](#Neh.7.55)). The father of some of the Nethinim.

Son of consolation, the surname of Joses, a Levite ([Acts 4:36](#Acts.4.36)). His name stands first on the list of prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch (13:1). Luke speaks of him as a “good man” (11:24). He was born of Jewish parents of the tribe of Levi. He was a native of Cyprus, where he had a possession of land ([Acts 4:36](#Acts.4.36), [37](#Acts.4.37)), which he sold. His personal appearance is supposed to have been dignified and commanding ([Acts 14:11](#Acts.14.11), [12](#Acts.14.12)). When Paul returned to Jerusalem after his conversion, Barnabas took him and introduced him to the apostles (9:27). They had probably been companions as students in the school of Gamaliel.

Surnamed Barsabas ([Acts 1:23](#Acts.1.23)); also called Justus. He was one of those who “companied with the apostles all the time that the Lord Jesus went out and in among them” ([Acts 1:21](#Acts.1.21)), and was one of the candidates for the place of Judas.

Son of Tolmai, one of the twelve apostles ([Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3); [Acts 1:13](#Acts.1.13)); generally supposed to have been the same as Nathanael. In the synoptic gospels Philip and Bartholomew are always mentioned together, while Nathanael is never mentioned; in the fourth gospel, on the other hand, Philip and Nathanael are similarly mentioned together, but nothing is said of Bartholomew. He was one of the disciples to whom our Lord appeared at the Sea of Tiberias after his resurrection ([John 21:2](#John.21.2)). He was also a witness of the Ascension ([Acts 1:4](#Acts.1.4), [12](#Acts.1.12), [13](#Acts.1.13)). He was an “Israelite indeed” ([John 1:47](#John.1.47)).
Son of Timaeus, one of the two blind beggars of Jericho ([Mark 10:46](#Mark.10.46); [Matt. 20:30](#Matt.20.30)). His blindness was miraculously cured on the ground of his faith.

The secretary of the prophet Jeremiah (32:12; 36:4). He was of the tribe of Judah (51:59). To him Jeremiah dictated his prophecies regarding the invasion of the Babylonians and the Captivity. These he read to the people from a window in the temple in the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah ([Jer. 36](#Jer.36)). He afterwards read them before the counsellors of the king at a private interview; and then to the king himself, who, after hearing a part of the roll, cut it with a penknife, and threw it into the fire of his winter parlour, where he was sitting.

A Gileadite of Rogelim who was distinguished for his loyalty to David. He liberally provided for the king’s followers ([2 Sam. 17:27](#2Sam.17.27)). David on his death-bed, remembering his kindness, commended Barzillai’s children to the care of Solomon ([1 Kings 2:7](#1Kgs.2.7)).
A priest who married a daughter of the preceding ([Ezra 2:61](#Ezra.2.61)).
A Meholathite, the father of Adriel ([2 Sam. 21:8](#2Sam.21.8)).

The daughter of Ishmael, the last of Esau’s three wives ([Gen. 36:3](#Gen.36.3), [4](#Gen.36.4), [13](#Gen.36.13)), from whose son Reuel four tribes of the Edomites sprung. She is also called Mahalath ([Gen. 28:9](#Gen.28.9)). It is noticeable that Esau’s three wives receive different names in the genealogical table of the Edomites ([Gen. 36](#Gen.36)) from those given to them in the history ([Gen. 26:34](#Gen.26.34); [28:9](#Gen.28.9)).

Daughter of the oath, or of seven, called also Bath-shu’a ([1 Chr. 3:5](#1Chr.3.5)), was the daughter of Eliam ([2 Sam. 11:3](#2Sam.11.3)) or Ammiel ([1 Chr. 3:5](#1Chr.3.5)), and wife of Uriah the Hittite. David committed adultery with her ([2 Sam. 11:4](#2Sam.11.4), [5](#2Sam.11.5); [Ps. 51:1](#Ps.51.1)). The child born in adultery died ([2 Sam. 12:15-19](#2Sam.12.15)). After her husband was slain (11:15) she was married to David (11:27), and became the mother of Solomon (12:24; [1 Kings 1:11](#1Kgs.1.11); [2:13](#1Kgs.2.13)). She took a prominent part in securing the succession of Solomon to the throne ([1 Kings 1:11](#1Kgs.1.11), [16-21](#1Kgs.1.16)).
Whose Lord is Jehovah, a Benjamite, one of David’s thirty heroes of the sling and bow ([1 Chr. 12:5](#1Chr.12.5)).

One of the judges of Israel ([1 Sam. 12:11](#1Sam.12.11)). It is uncertain who he was. Some suppose that Barak is meant, others Samson, but most probably this is a contracted form of Abdon ([Judg. 12:13](#Judg.12.13)).
The father of Judith, one of the wives of Esau ([Gen. 26:34](#Gen.26.34)), the same as Adah ([Gen. 36:2](#Gen.36.2)).
The son of Beor, and a king of Edom ([Gen. 36:32](#Gen.36.32), [33](#Gen.36.33); [1 Chr. 1:43](#1Chr.1.43)).

Bel protect the king!, the last of the kings of Babylon ([Dan. 5:1](#Dan.5.1)). He was the son of Nabonidus by Nitocris, who was the daughter of Nebuchadnezzar and the widow of Nergal-sharezer. When still young he made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and when heated with wine sent for the sacred vessels his “father” ([Dan. 5:2](#Dan.5.2)), or grandfather, Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from the temple in Jerusalem, and he and his princes drank out of them. …
Son of my kindred; i.e., “born of incest”, the son of Lot by his youngest daughter ([Gen. 19:38](#Gen.19.38)).
The king of Syria whom Asa, king of Judah, employed to invade Israel ([1 Kings 15:18](#1Kgs.15.18)).
King of Damascus, and successor of his father Hazael on the throne of Syria ([2 Kings 13:3](#2Kgs.13.3), [4](#2Kgs.13.4)). His misfortunes in war are noticed by Amos (1:4).

Son of the preceding, also king of Syria. He was long engaged in war against Israel. He was murdered probably by Hazael, by whom he was succeeded ([2 Kings 8:7-15](#2Kgs.8.7)), after a reign of some thirty years.

The son of Jehoiada, chief priest ([1 Chr. 27:5](#1Chr.27.5)). He was set by David over his body-guard of Cherethites and Pelethites ([2 Sam. 8:18](#2Sam.8.18); [1 Kings 1:32](#1Kgs.1.32); [1 Chr. 18:17](#1Chr.18.17)). His exploits are enumerated in [2 Sam. 23:20](#2Sam.23.20), [21](#2Sam.23.21), [22](#2Sam.23.22); [1 Chr. 11:22](#1Chr.11.22). He remained faithful to Solomon ([1 Kings 1:8](#1Kgs.1.8), [10](#1Kgs.1.10), [26](#1Kgs.1.26)), by whom he was raised to the rank of commander-in-chief ([1 Kings 2:25](#1Kgs.2.25), [29](#1Kgs.2.29), [30](#1Kgs.2.30), [34](#1Kgs.2.34), [35](#1Kgs.2.35); [4:4](#1Kgs.4.4)).
